claims.source: BBS9 can be divided into an N-terminal ß-propeller domain (residues 1–368) and a C-terminal part containing predicted GAE, platform and alpha-helical domains (residues 363–887) (Jin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2010 and domain predictions.

claims.claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 forms a complex with BBS5.
claims.source: We could isolate complexes of BBS5 with the N-terminal ß-propeller (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and of BBS1 with the C-terminal part.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The C-terminal part of BBS9 forms a complex with BBS1.
claims.source: We could isolate complexes of BBS5 with the N-terminal ß-propeller (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and of BBS1 with the C-terminal part.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The C-terminal part of BBS9 elutes as a dimeric species in gel filtration.
claims.source: Consistent with the study of Knockenhauer et al. (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015), we found the C-terminal part of BBS9 to elute as a dimeric species in gel filtration, while the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and a citation to Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015.

claims.claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer in gel filtration.
claims.source: Consistent with the study of Knockenhauer et al. (Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015), we found the C-terminal part of BBS9 to elute as a dimeric species in gel filtration, while the N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 runs as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Full length BBS9 preserves dimerization at high concentrations but shifts to lower molecular weight at lower concentrations.
claims.source: We find that full length BBS9 preserves dimerization at high concentrations, but the elution peak shifts to lower molecular weight at lower concentrations.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of BBS9 gel filtration behavior.

claims.claim: BBS18 dramatically improved the yield of soluble complexes when introduced into complexes with BBS1,5,8 and 9.
claims.source: The introduction of the 10 kDa protein BBS18 however dramatically improved the yield of soluble complexes, as in a complex with BBS1,5,8 and 9.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex solubility.

claims.claim: BBS18 is crucial to link BBS4 to the complex containing BBS1,5,8,9.
claims.source: We also found BBS18 to be crucial to link BBS4 to this complex, which is consistent with an interaction of BBS18 with both BBS4 and with BBS8,9.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and inference from complex formation patterns.

claims.claim: Coexpression of the full ensemble of eight BBSome subunits yielded only small amounts of complex with substoichiometric amounts of BBS2 and BBS7.
claims.source: Coexpression of the full ensemble of eight BBSome subunits yielded only small amounts of complex with substoichiometric amounts of BBS2 and BBS7 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claims.claim: The full BBSome was difficult to purify and ran as oligomeric species on gel filtration.
claims.source: This full BBSome was difficult to purify and ran as oligomeric species on gel filtration.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of full BBSome purification.

claims.claim: Complexes containing BBS18 but not BBS2 and 7 had greatly improved stability and do not oligomerize.
claims.source: Instead we found that complexes containing BBS18 but not BBS2 and 7 had a greatly improved stability and do not oligomerize.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex stability.

claims.claim: The largest and most stable subcomplex is composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 18.
claims.source: The largest and most stable subcomplex is composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9 and 18.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex stability.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome retains most of the functionality of the full BBSome machinery known so far.
claims.source: We consider this a BBSome core complex since it shows the most promising structural and functional properties, as it retains most of the functionality of the full BBSome machinery known so far.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations and inference from functional assays.

claims.claim: Coexpression with BBS chaperonins BBS6, 10 and 12 did not improve sample quality of BBSome subcomplexes or the full BBSome.
claims.source: Of note, we did not observe any additional improvement of sample quality of BBSome subcomplexes or the full BBSome upon coexpression with any or all of the BBS chaperonins BBS6, 10 and 12.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of co-expression effects.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome could be purified in milligram quantities.
claims.source: The 6mer core BBSome could readily be purified in milligram quantities, and is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of purification yields.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
claims.source: The 6mer core BBSome could readily be purified in milligram quantities, and is soluble up to concentrations higher than 150 µM (>50 mg/ml).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of protein solubility.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome complex was resistant to high salt washes of up to 2.5 M NaCl.
claims.source: The complex eluted as a single entity in all subsequent purification steps (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), and was even resistant to high salt washes of up to 2.5 M NaCl, consistent with a previous study where the native BBSome was eluted with high salt concentrations from an Arl6 affinity column (Jin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa.
claims.source: The complex elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, in acceptable agreement with the expected theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), but less consistent with it being a dimer.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claims.claim: The theoretical mass of the 6mer core BBSome is 336.4 kDa.
claims.source: The complex elutes in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, in acceptable agreement with the expected theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), but less consistent with it being a dimer.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the known molecular weights of the subunits.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome has a distorted Y-shape with pseudo 3-fold symmetry.
claims.source: The complex has a distorted Y-shape (side view) with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture, although we cannot identify the localization of individual subunits at this resolution.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data and 3-D reconstruction.

claims.claim: The 6mer core BBSome has a loosely packed architecture.
claims.source: The complex has a distorted Y-shape (side view) with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture, although we cannot identify the localization of individual subunits at this resolution.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data and 3-D reconstruction.

claims.claim: The 3-D reconstruction of the core BBSome has a resolution of ~23 Å.
claims.source: The final resolution of the reconstructed model was 23 Å, as estimated by Fourier shell correlation (criterion of 0.5).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on electron microscopy data analysis.

claims.claim: The 6mer BBSome core was captured by Arl6•GppNHp in a nucleotide-dependent manner.
claims.source: In pulldown experiments with immobilized Arl6, the purified 6mer BBSome core was captured in a nucleotide-dependent manner: While a 7.5 fold molar excess of Arl6•GppNHp precipitated the major part of the BBSome from solution, Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity, which supports the notion that the BBsome is the effector of Arl6 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity for the 6mer BBSome core.
claims.source: In pulldown experiments with immobilized Arl6, the purified 6mer BBSome core was captured in a nucleotide-dependent manner: While a 7.5 fold molar excess of Arl6•GppNHp precipitated the major part of the BBSome from solution, Arl6•GDP had no detectable affinity, which supports the notion that the BBsome is the effector of Arl6 (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The core BBSome binds to a truncated Smo receptor fragment (residues R546-L665).
claims.source: To test whether the core BBSome can recognize known BBSome cargo proteins, we generated a truncated (residues R546-L665) version of the Smo receptor, which contains a ciliary targeting motif predicted to interact with the BBSome (Zhang et al., 2012a; Seo et al., 2011; Corbit et al., 2005). In pulldown experiments as described above (Figure 3), the binding was clearly detectable, but considerably weaker than that of Arl6•GppNHp.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: The affinity of the core BBSome for fluoresceine-labeled Smo(R546-L665) is 36.1 ± 3.9 µM.
claims.source: In fluorescence polarization experiments (see below), we determined the affinity for a fluoresceine-labeled version of this Smo fragment to be 36.1 ± 3.9 µM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization experiments.

claims.claim: The core BBSome has the strongest interaction with peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminal region of SSTR3.
claims.source: A quantification of the signal intensities from the microarray (Figure 4C) indicates that the core BBSome has the strongest interaction with peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminal region of SSTR3, indicated in blue and green in the intensity diagram and in the context of the snake plot of SSTR3 (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claims.claim: The core BBSome binds to peptides from potential BBSome cargo proteins including GPCRs.
claims.source: We found BBSome binding motifs in most of the GPCRs tested and in Polycystin-1, Polycystin-2, the leptin receptor and Fibrocystin (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Significant BBSome-GPCR binding was almost exclusively observed for peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminus.
claims.source: Significant BBSome-GPCR binding was almost exclusively observed for peptides from the 3ICL and the C-terminus, which are the regions previously described to interact with the BBSome and to contain ciliary targeting sequences like Ax(S/A)xQ (Berbari et al., 2008a) or (I/V)KARK (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013) in the 3ICL or a (F/Y/W)(K/R) motif in the C-terminal part (Corbit et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior studies on CTS sequences.

claims.claim: The interactions with Polycystin-1 correspond to a region of 44 residues that contains a tyrosine-based sorting signal YEMV.
claims.source: The interactions with Polycystin-1 correspond to a region of 44 residues that was shown to be important for ciliary targeting and that contains a tyrosine-based sorting signal YEMV (Su et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Su et al., 2015.

claims.claim: No interactions were observed with the VxPx ciliary targeting signals from the C-terminus of Polycystin-1 and Rhodopsin or the RVxP motif in the N-terminal domain of Polycystin-2.
claims.source: Finally, no interactions were observed with the VxPx ciliary targeting signals from the C-terminus of Polycystin-1 and Rhodopsin or the RVxP motif in the N-terminal domain of Polycystin-2 (Geng et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Geng et al., 2006.

claims.claim: Multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities for the BBSome were identified.
claims.source: Sequence analysis of the binding peptides revealed no unique, single consensus motif for BBSome binding. Instead, we identified multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities for the BBSome (see below).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental data from peptide arrays and fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: Dissociation constants (KD) of <25 µM were determined for the majority of the tested peptides.
claims.source: As summarized in Table 1, we determined dissociation constants (KD) of <25 µM for the majority of the tested peptides.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data summarized in Table 1.

claims.claim: SSTR3 CT1 peptide from the C-terminus had an affinity of 22.1 ± 1.4 µM.
claims.source: From the 15mer peptides of SSTR3 identified in the microarray screen, SSTR3 CT1 from the C-terminus had the highest affinity (22.1 ± 1.4 µM).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: Elongation of SSTR3 CT1 by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2) increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM.
claims.source: Elongation of this peptide by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2), which includes three residues from the 7th transmembrane region and 21 residues from the C-terminus, increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM, the highest of all tested peptides.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: SSTR3 CT2 had the highest affinity of all tested peptides (0.11 ± 0.02 µM).
claims.source: Elongation of this peptide by nine residues (SSTR3 CT2), which includes three residues from the 7th transmembrane region and 21 residues from the C-terminus, increased the affinity to 0.11 ± 0.02 µM, the highest of all tested peptides.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: The peptide SSTR3-3ICL from the third intracellular loop of SSTR3 had an affinity of 12.8 ± 1.0 μM.
claims.source: The peptide SSTR3-3ICL from the third intracellular loop of SSTR3 had an affinity of 12.8 ± 1.0 μM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: Smo CT1 and Smo CT4 bound with affinities of 1.8 ± 0.5 μM and 1.1 ± 0.5 μM, respectively.
claims.source: The identified 15mer peptide Smo CT1 and a slightly elongated 19mer Smo CT4 bound with affinities of 1.8 ± 0.5 μM and 1.1 ± 0.5 μM, respectively, to core BBSome.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: Smo CT2, which contains one of two polybasic sequences in the C-terminal cytosolic region of Smoothened, bound only weakly with an affinity of >100 μM.
claims.source: Smo CT2, which contains one of two polybasic sequences in the C-terminal cytosolic region of Smoothened, bound only weakly, with an affinity of >100 μM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: The 37mer peptide Smo CT3 that spans both sequences of SMO CT1 and CT2 had an affinity of 1.4 ± 0.5 μM.
claims.source: Consistently, the 37mer peptide Smo CT3 that spans both sequences of SMO CT1 and CT2 had an affinity of 1.4 ± 0.5 μM, which is similar to that of Smo CT1 alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: A second polybasic sequence KRLGRKKKRRKRKKE in the C-terminal region of Smoothened (Smo CT8) had an affinity of 6.8 ± 2.5 µM.
claims.source: A second polybasic sequence KRLGRKKKRRKRKKE in the C-terminal region of Smoothened (Smo CT8) had a significant affinity of 6.8 ± 2.5 µM, although it is much lower than Smo CT4.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: GPR161 3ICL peptide had an affinity of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM.
claims.source: Of these, the peptides GPR161 3ICL and NMU 3ICL1 had significant affinities of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM and 18.1 ± 1.6 µM, respectively, while the other tested peptides only presented low affinities of >50 µM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: NMU 3ICL1 peptide had an affinity of 18.1 ± 1.6 µM.
claims.source: Of these, the peptides GPR161 3ICL and NMU 3ICL1 had significant affinities of 6.3 ± 1.5 µM and 18.1 ± 1.6 µM, respectively, while the other tested peptides only presented low affinities of >50 µM.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: Mutations of epitopes with basic and aromatic residues reduce BBSome binding affinity significantly.
claims.source: For both Smo and SSTR3 we can show that mutations of epitopes with basic and aromatic residues reduce BBSome binding affinity significantly, but that there is no simple universal binding motif at least for these two GPCRs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis using fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: For SSTR3, the affinity is derived from all three motifs (YR, FK, and FRR) and is somewhat additive.
claims.source: In the case of SSTR3 we targeted the three epitopes YR, FK and FRR, which were mutated to alanine in various combinations. It appears that the affinity is derived from all three motifs and is somewhat additive.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: Mutation of two residues from each SSTR3 motif changes affinity between four and fourtenfold.
claims.source: Mutation of two residues from each motif changes affinity between four and fourtenfold, whereas combinations with four or six mutated residues reduce affinity up to ~100 fold.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: Mutation of three arginine residues at the C-terminus of peptide SSTR3 CT2 (RRVR, residues 333–336, mutated to EEVE) reduces affinity 42 fold.
claims.source: The binding site is even more complex, since mutation of three arginine residues at the C-terminus of peptide SSTR3 CT2, that do not strictly follow a (F/Y/W)(K/R) annotation (RRVR, residues 333–336, mutated to EEVE), also reduces affinity 42 fold.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: Mutation of either the WRR or the WCR motif in Smo CT4 changes affinity 9 and 11 fold, respectively.
claims.source: The mutation of either the WRR or the WCR motif changes affinity 9 and 11 fold, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: The combined quadruple variant of Smo CT4 reduces affinity 13 fold.
claims.source: The combined quadruple variant reduces affinity 13 fold, again demonstrating that an extended epitope is recognized by the BBsome.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: Arl6•GppNHp does not significantly affect the binding of cargo peptides to the core BBSome.
claims.source: We thus tested the binding of cargo in the presence of Arl6•GppNHp, but did not find significant Arl6 dependency in our fluorescence polarization assay. By titrating either the core BBSome alone or a stoichiometric mixture of the core BBSome with Arl6•GppNHp to fluorescently labeled peptides SSTR3 CT1, SSTR3 CT2 and SSTR3 3ICL, no significant difference in binding behavior was observed (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The core BBSome represents the complete set of BBSome subunits for which analogs are found in Drosophila.
claims.source: The core BBSome as the most stable of the complexes analyzed in our studies, composed of BBS 1,4,5,8, 9 and 18, represents the complete set of BBSome subunits for which analogs are found in Drosophila (Nachury et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nachury et al., 2007 and knowledge of Drosophila BBSome composition.

claims.claim: BBS2 and BBS7 are absent in Drosophila and might be dispensable for many aspects of BBSome function.
claims.source: BBS2 and BBS7 are absent in Drosophila and might therefore be dispensable for many aspects of BBSome function.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Drosophila lacks these subunits but has functional cilia.

claims.claim: BBS2 and BBS7 are dispensable for the formation of a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
claims.source: It appears that they are at least dispensable for the formation of a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that the core BBSome lacking BBS2 and BBS7 can bind cargo and Arl6.

claims.claim: The observed formation of a stable core BBSome is in contrast to previous studies suggesting that BBS6, 10 and 12 are required for BBSome formation.
claims.source: The observed formation of a stable core BBSome is in contrast to previous co-immunoprecipitation and co-migration experiments which suggested that BBS6, 10 and 12 are required for BBSome formation (Seo et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of current experimental results with prior literature.

claims.claim: BBS7 and BBS2 reduce the solubility of the entire BBSome complex.
claims.source: We observed that BBS7 and BBS2, which are highly insoluble proteins by themselves, also reduce the solubility of the entire BBSome complex, in the presence or absence of BBS6, 10 and 12 or any combinations thereof.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of complex solubility.

claims.claim: The CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome.
claims.source: We propose that the CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome, which might not operate in insect cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible role for chaperonines.

claims.claim: The assembly of the BBSome might follow two parallel routes.
claims.source: We propose that the CCT/TRiC complex and the chaperonines might have a role in folding BBS7 and BBS2 before these proteins are added to the BBSome, which might not operate in insect cells. Nevertheless, the formation of the 6mer BBSome indicates that the assembly might follow two parallel routes, one assembling the core BBSome and the second via the BBS/CCT complex to deliver BBS7 and probably also BBS2 to the complex.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a model for BBSome assembly based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: The insect cell expression machinery is sufficient for folding and assembly of an active core BBSome.
claims.source: In conclusion, the insect cell expression machinery seems to be sufficient for folding and assembly of an active core BBSome.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations that the core BBSome can be produced in insect cells.

claims.claim: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain of BBS9 binds to BBS5 and the C-terminal appendage part forms a stable complex with BBS1.
claims.source: The N-terminal ß-propeller domain (residues 1–368) of BBS9 binds to BBS5 and the C-terminal appendage part forms a stable complex with BBS1.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of domain-specific interactions.

claims.claim: Two of the lobes of the Y-shaped structure contain BBS1 and BBS5, respectively, while the third lobe includes BBS4, 8 and 18.
claims.source: We therefore assume that two of the lobes of the Y contain BBS1 and BBS5, respectively, while the third lobe includes the three remaining proteins BBS4, 8 and 18.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from interaction data and EM structure.

claims.claim: BBS9 may hold the assembly together as either a monomer or a dimer.
claims.source: BBS9 may hold the assembly together as either a monomer or a dimer.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative about the oligomeric state of BBS9 in the complex.

claims.claim: The core BBSome binds to activated GTP-bound Arl6, but not to Arl6•GDP.
claims.source: We could demonstrate that the core BBSome binds to activated GTP-bound Arl6, but not to Arl6•GDP.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from pulldown assays.

claims.claim: The Arl6 interaction only requires the BBS1 ß-propeller.
claims.source: While the Arl6 interaction only requires the BBS1 ß-propeller (Mourão et al., 2014), the interaction with cargo might require the complete BBS1 protein and/or additional BBSome components.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mourão et al., 2014.

claims.claim: A small peptide fragment from the C-terminal part of SSTR3 binds to the core BBSome with ~110 nM affinity, while the affinity to BBS1 (aa1-430) is ~100 fold lower.
claims.source: Indeed, we were able to identify a small peptide fragment from the C-terminal part of SSTR3 which binds to the core BBSome with ~110 nM affinity, while the affinity to BBS1 (aa1-430) is ~100 fold lower (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The 3ICL of SSTR3 has similar affinities to the truncated BBS1 subunit and the core BBSome.
claims.source: In contrast, the 3ICL of SSTR3 has similar affinities to the truncated BBS1 subunit and the core BBSome.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from fluorescence polarization.

claims.claim: The C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome.
claims.source: These findings might indicate that, while the C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome, the interaction with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding affinities observed.

claims.claim: The interaction of SSTR3 with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
claims.source: These findings might indicate that, while the C-terminal domain of SSTR3 requires interactions with BBS1 and other subunits of the core BBSome, the interaction with its 3ICL is mostly mediated by BBS1 alone.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding affinities observed.

claims.claim: A GST-tagged 3ICL of SSTR3 binds strongly to BBS1, but less prominently to BBS4,5,8 and 9.
claims.source: The latter is consistent with the previous finding that a GST-tagged 3ICL of SSTR3 binds strongly to BBS1, but less prominently to BBS4,5,8 and 9 (Jin et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The 3ICL of SSTR3 is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia.
claims.source: It was also shown that the 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia (Berbari et al., 2008a), but that removing this loop from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008a.

claims.claim: Removing the 3ICL from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
claims.source: It was also shown that the 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia (Berbari et al., 2008a), but that removing this loop from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Berbari et al., 2008a.

claims.claim: The microarray data suggested no significant binding of the BBSome to the 3ICL of Smoothened.
claims.source: For Smoothened, our microarray data suggested no significant binding of the BBSome to its 3ICL, but instead to three sequences within its C-terminal region.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from peptide microarrays.

claims.claim: Deletion of the 17 residue polybasic motif in Smoothened had minimal effect on BBS1 binding.
claims.source: This finding is consistent with a previous study which indicated BBS1 interaction with the Smo region Q477-L665 containing all three motifs found in the microarray, but deletion of the 17 residue polybasic motif had minimal effect on BBS1 binding (Zhang et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2012a.

claims.claim: Deletion of the second, 10 residue polybasic stretch from the C-terminus of Smoothened enhanced binding to BBS1.
claims.source: In that study, a deletion of the second, 10 residue polybasic stretch from the C-terminus of Smoothened was found to enhance binding to BBS1, which indicates a possible regulatory role of this region.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claims.claim: Neither of the polybasic motifs in Smoothened strongly affect the ciliary localization of Smoothened.
claims.source: It was found that neither of the polybasic motifs are strongly affecting the ciliary localization of Smoothened (Nedelcu, 2013), supporting the notion that binding to BBSome and ciliary localization are not necessarily overlapping features.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nedelcu, 2013.

claims.claim: The BBSome may contain an extended binding site for target molecules that recognizes general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence.
claims.source: Thus we would assume that the BBSome may contain an extended binding site for target molecules that recognizes general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from mutational analysis data.

claims.claim: Enhanced BBSome binding almost invariantly started when the peptide walk approached an arginine residue in the corresponding region.
claims.source: By performing a single-residue walk over the GPCR sequence we can show that enhanced BBSome binding almost invariantly started when the peptide walk approached an arginine residue in the corresponding region.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from peptide microarrays.

claims.claim: All tested GPCRs contain an arginine residue close to the N-terminal start of the 3ICL.
claims.source: We observed that arginine-rich motifs enhancing BBSome binding are also present in the 3ICL: All tested GPCRs contain an arginine residue close to the N-terminal start of the 3ICL, and peptides containing this arginine have a strong tendency to enhanced BBSome binding.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis and experimental observations.

claims.claim: CTS sequences that do not contain a clustering of aromatic and basic residues don't seem to be sufficient to bind to the core BBSome.
claims.source: In contrast, we found that CTS sequences that do not contain a clustering of aromatic and basic residues, such as the Ax(S/A)xQ motif (Bhogaraju et al., 2013) of MCHR1 and SSTR3 as well as an (I/V)KARK motif from GPCR 161 (Bhogaraju et al., 2013; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2013) don't seem to be sufficient to bind to the core BBSome: Although we found peptides that overlap with or are in close proximity to these CTS motifs, enhanced binding to the core BBSome does not require the CTS sequence being part of the peptide.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from peptide microarrays and citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing the affinity to the core BBSome.
claims.source: We observed that multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing the affinity to the core BBSome, which explains why a single denominator for BBSome interactions is hard to identify.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations from mutational analysis.

claims.claim: BBSome binding and ciliary targeting are not necessarily related in a simple fashion.

claims.claim: For certain proteins the BBSome has been shown to be more important for the export phase of ciliary transport rather than its import.
claims.source: At least for certain proteins the BBSome has been shown to be more important for the export phase of ciliary transport (Lechtreck et al., 2013; Liew et al., 2014) rather than its import, indicating that different signals might exist for import, retention or export of BBSome cargo.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lechtreck et al., 2013 and Liew et al., 2014.

results.result: Individual BBSome subunits were expressed in insect cells, but most showed poor solubility. Only BBS5, BBS9, and BBS18 were soluble in significant amounts when expressed individually, while other subunits co-purified with chaperones or were degraded.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B. The SDS-PAGE gels clearly demonstrate expression of all subunits and differential solubility, with most subunits requiring co-expression for stability.

results.result: Co-expression studies identified stabilizing binary interactions between BBSome subunits. BBS9 emerged as a central organizational component forming stable interactions with BBS1, 2, 5, and 8. BBS18 with BBS4 and BBS9 with BBS8 showed the strongest solubility improvements. BBS chaperonins BBS6 and BBS12 stabilized each other but did not improve BBSome subunit yields.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing purified binary and multimeric complexes. The interaction network is consistent with prior immunoprecipitation studies (C35 cites Katoh et al., 2015), providing converging evidence for the proposed architecture.

results.result: BBS9 can be divided into an N-terminal β-propeller domain (residues 1-368) and a C-terminal domain (residues 363-887) with distinct binding specificities. The N-terminal domain binds BBS5 as a monomer, while the C-terminal domain binds BBS1 and forms dimers in gel filtration. Full-length BBS9 shows concentration-dependent dimerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C43 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing gel filtration profiles and complex formation. The domain boundaries are consistent with prior structural predictions (Jin et al., 2010) and the dimerization behavior agrees with Knockenhauer and Schwartz, 2015.

results.result: A stable heterohexameric core BBSome complex composed of BBS1, 4, 5, 8, 9, and 18 was identified. BBS18 dramatically improved complex solubility and is crucial for linking BBS4 to the complex. The full 8-subunit BBSome with BBS2 and BBS7 was poorly soluble and oligomeric, while the 6-mer core was stable and monomeric. BBS chaperonins did not improve complex quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 are supported by extensive biochemical data in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The gel filtration, SDS-PAGE, and purification data clearly demonstrate the superior stability of the 6-mer core over the full 8-mer complex. This is a key finding of the manuscript.

results.result: The 6-mer core BBSome could be purified in milligram quantities with high solubility (>150 µM or >50 mg/ml). The complex was resistant to high salt washes up to 2.5 M NaCl and eluted in gel filtration with an apparent molecular weight of ~400 kDa, consistent with the theoretical mass of 336.4 kDa for a monomer.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E. The gel filtration profile, salt resistance, and purification yields demonstrate the exceptional stability of the core complex. The apparent MW is slightly higher than theoretical but within acceptable range for gel filtration, arguing against dimerization.

results.result: Negative stain electron microscopy revealed that the 6-mer core BBSome has a distorted Y-shape with pseudo 3-fold symmetry and a loosely packed architecture. The 3-D reconstruction achieved a resolution of ~23 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by EM data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The 2-D class averages and 3-D reconstruction clearly show the Y-shaped architecture. The resolution of 23 Å is appropriate for negative stain EM and was determined by standard FSC criteria.

results.result: The 6-mer core BBSome binds to Arl6•GppNHp in a nucleotide-dependent manner, with no detectable binding to Arl6•GDP, confirming the BBSome as an effector of Arl6.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by pulldown data in Figure 3. The nucleotide-dependent binding is clearly demonstrated, with Arl6•GppNHp capturing most of the BBSome while Arl6•GDP shows no binding. This is consistent with the known role of Arl6 in BBSome recruitment.

results.result: The core BBSome binds to a truncated Smo receptor fragment (residues R546-L665) containing a ciliary targeting motif. The binding was detectable in pulldown assays but weaker than Arl6•GppNHp, with an affinity of 36.1 ± 3.9 µM measured by fluorescence polarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C63 are supported by pulldown data in Figure 3 and fluorescence polarization measurements. The binding is clearly detectable but weaker than Arl6, consistent with the micromolar affinities typical of cargo-adapter interactions. The quantitative measurement provides important validation.

results.result: Peptide microarray screening identified BBSome binding sites in multiple cargo proteins. The core BBSome binds most strongly to peptides from the 3ICL and C-terminal regions of SSTR3 and other GPCRs, as well as to specific regions in Polycystin-1 containing a YEMV sorting signal. No binding was observed to VxPx or RVxP ciliary targeting signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 are supported by peptide microarray data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The screening approach is unbiased and identifies binding regions consistent with prior literature on CTS sequences. The negative results for VxPx motifs are important controls showing specificity.

results.result: Fluorescence polarization measurements validated peptide microarray hits and determined dissociation constants. Multiple binding epitopes with variable affinities were identified. SSTR3 CT2 showed the highest affinity (0.11 ± 0.02 µM), while most tested peptides had KD values <25 µM. Smo peptides bound with affinities ranging from 1.1 to >100 µM depending on the region.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C80 are supported by extensive fluorescence polarization data in Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Table 1. The quantitative measurements validate the microarray results and reveal a range of affinities consistent with multiple binding modes. The data quality appears good with error estimates provided.

results.result: Mutational analysis of SSTR3 and Smo peptides showed that mutations of aromatic and basic residues significantly reduce BBSome binding affinity. For SSTR3, affinity is derived from three motifs (YR, FK, FRR) in an additive manner, with mutations reducing affinity 4-100 fold. For Smo, mutations of WRR or WCR motifs reduced affinity 9-13 fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 are supported by mutational analysis data in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The systematic mutagenesis demonstrates that multiple aromatic/basic residues contribute to binding, with additive effects. This provides strong evidence for an extended binding site rather than a single consensus motif.

results.result: Arl6•GppNHp does not significantly affect the binding of cargo peptides (SSTR3 CT1, CT2, 3ICL) to the core BBSome in fluorescence polarization assays.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A showing overlapping binding curves for BBSome alone versus BBSome + Arl6•GppNHp. This suggests Arl6 and cargo binding sites do not overlap or allosterically regulate each other, though the authors acknowledge this is based on peptide fragments.

results.result: The 6-mer core BBSome represents the complete set of BBSome subunits found in Drosophila, which lacks BBS2 and BBS7. These subunits appear dispensable for forming a stable monomeric complex that interacts with cargo and Arl6.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by the experimental demonstration that the 6-mer core (lacking BBS2/7) binds both Arl6 and cargo, combined with knowledge that Drosophila lacks these subunits but has functional cilia. This provides evolutionary support for the functional sufficiency of the core complex.

results.result: The formation of a stable core BBSome without BBS chaperonins contrasts with prior studies suggesting BBS6, 10, and 12 are required for BBSome assembly. The authors propose that chaperonins may fold BBS2/7 before addition to the BBSome, a process that may not operate in insect cells, and that BBSome assembly might follow two parallel routes.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 mix supported observations (C91-C92 based on experimental data) with speculative proposals (C93-C94). While the core BBSome formation without chaperonins is clearly demonstrated, the proposed dual assembly pathway is speculative and not directly tested. The insect cell system may not fully recapitulate mammalian assembly.

results.result: Based on domain-specific interactions and EM structure, the authors propose that the Y-shaped core BBSome has BBS1 and BBS5 in two lobes, with BBS4, 8, and 18 in the third lobe, held together by BBS9 as either a monomer or dimer.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C98 are partially supported (C96 by experimental data on domain interactions) but largely speculative (C97-C98). The 23 Å resolution EM structure cannot localize individual subunits, so the proposed arrangement is inference from biochemical data. The oligomeric state of BBS9 in the complex remains unclear.

results.result: The core BBSome binds Arl6•GTP but not Arl6•GDP, with the interaction requiring only the BBS1 β-propeller. Cargo binding shows differential requirements: SSTR3 C-terminus requires the full core BBSome (110 nM affinity) with ~100-fold lower affinity to BBS1 alone, while SSTR3 3ICL binds similarly to BBS1 alone and the core BBSome, suggesting the C-terminus requires multiple subunits while 3ICL binding is primarily BBS1-mediated.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C105 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5B and pulldown assays, combined with citations to prior work on Arl6-BBS1 interaction. The differential binding requirements for different SSTR3 regions provide important mechanistic insight into cargo recognition complexity.

results.result: Prior studies showed SSTR3 3ICL is sufficient to target non-ciliary GPCRs to cilia but removing it from SSTR3 does not prevent ciliary localization. For Smoothened, microarray data showed no significant BBSome binding to 3ICL but binding to C-terminal sequences. Prior studies found deletion of the 17-residue polybasic motif had minimal effect on BBS1 binding, while deletion of the 10-residue polybasic stretch enhanced binding. Neither polybasic motif strongly affects Smoothened ciliary localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C111 accurately summarize prior literature (Berbari et al., 2008a; Zhang et al., 2012a; Nedelcu, 2013) and integrate it with the current microarray findings. This demonstrates that BBSome binding and ciliary localization are not simply correlated, an important conceptual point.

results.result: The BBSome contains an extended binding site recognizing general features of aromatic and basic residues rather than a specific sequence. Peptide walks showed enhanced binding when approaching arginine residues, with all tested GPCRs containing an arginine near the N-terminal start of the 3ICL. CTS sequences lacking aromatic/basic clustering (Ax(S/A)xQ, (I/V)KARK) were insufficient for core BBSome binding. Multiple aromatic/basic stretches are additive in enhancing affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C116 are supported by comprehensive peptide microarray data, mutational analysis, and sequence analysis. The conclusion of an extended binding site with additive contributions from multiple motifs is well-supported by the experimental evidence, though the claim remains somewhat speculative (C112) in proposing the general mechanism.

results.result: BBSome binding and ciliary targeting are not simply related. The BBSome is more important for export than import for certain proteins. The authors propose CTS might function as ciliary retention signals, with final protein localization determined by equilibrium of interactions inside and outside the cilium, which is dynamic and depends on signaling (e.g., Hedgehog pathway dramatically changes Smo and Ptch localization).
results.evaluation: Claims C117-C121 mix supported observations from prior literature (C118, C121 with citations) with speculative proposals (C119-C120). While the disconnect between BBSome binding and ciliary localization is well-documented, the proposed retention signal mechanism is speculative and not directly tested in this study.

results.result: The study identified a stable heterohexameric BBSome core complex that binds GPCRs with interactions only partially overlapping with previously described CTS, indicating more complex recognition than anticipated. Arl6•GTP does not affect BBSome-cargo interactions, suggesting no direct involvement in cargo loading/unloading. This stable complex enables future detailed biochemical and structural analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C126 accurately summarize the major findings of the manuscript. The core complex identification (C123), partial CTS overlap (C124), and lack of Arl6 effect on cargo binding (C125-C126) are all well-supported by the experimental data. C122 is a forward-looking statement about future work enabled by this study.
